terms.description: An AI system able to learn, reason, and apply knowledge across a wide range of tasks and domains at or beyond human level.
AI built to act as an autonomous or semi-autonomous agent that interprets goals, plans steps, uses tools such as browsers, code, or APIs, learns from feedback, and adapts to finish tasks.
Ensuring an AI system's goals and behavior match what people truly intend, including their values and rules.
Standardized tests for measuring and comparing AI systems on tasks such as answering questions, recognizing images, writing code, or following instructions.
The ability to work with AI productively and responsibly by understanding its strengths and limits, judging its outputs critically, using it ethically, and adapting as it changes.
The field concerned with making AI systems behave reliably and avoid harm, even when they are powerful, widely used, or in unexpected situations.
The integrated combination of software, hardware, and computing resources that supports every stage of the AI lifecycle.
terms.note: The source page text was cut off for this entry, so the description is completed from its visible part and general meaning.

terms.description: The end-to-end process of building, deploying, and maintaining an AI system, from data collection and preparation through training, testing, and deployment.
A step-by-step set of instructions for solving a problem or completing a task, much like a recipe.
The situation where many organizations rely on the same or very similar AI programs, algorithms, or training data.
A network of AI systems or agents that share information and coordinate their actions as a group.
terms.note: The source page text was cut off for this entry, so the description is completed from its visible part and general meaning.

terms.description: A term coined in 1955 by Stanford's first AI faculty member, John McCarthy, who described the field as the science and engineering of making intelligent machines.
A neural network method that helps a model focus on the most relevant parts of its input when producing an output.
Technology, including AI, carrying out specific tasks according to explicit human instructions and predefined parameters.
The way neural networks learn from mistakes by working backward through the network to find which parts caused the error.
Graphical models that use probabilities to show cause-and-effect relationships among variables, like a map of how factors influence one another.
When an AI system produces results that favor or discriminate against certain groups of people.
Datasets so large that traditional data-processing software cannot handle them, but that AI can analyze to reveal patterns and trends.
A program designed to simulate conversation with humans through text or voice.
Also called proprietary software; software whose code is restricted and not open to the public to view, modify, or use.
The AI field that lets computers see, identify, and understand visual information from images and videos.
The amount of input, such as text, that an AI system can process at one time during a task.
A machine learning technique where a model learns what makes things alike or different by comparing similar and dissimilar examples.
Expanding a training dataset by creating modified versions of existing data instead of collecting new data.
Discovering patterns and trends in large datasets using statistical methods and machine learning.
An attack where an adversary inserts, alters, or mislabels data in a model's training set to corrupt what it learns.

terms.description: A machine learning algorithm that makes predictions by asking a series of yes/no questions that split the data by feature until it reaches a conclusion.
A subset of machine learning that uses large multi-layer neural networks to automatically learn complex patterns from data.
Generative models that create new content, such as images, by adding noise to data and then learning to remove it.
Simplifying complex data by cutting the number of variables while keeping the most important information.
Numerical vector representations of data such as words or images that capture their meaning or characteristics.
Techniques that combine multiple models, often called weak learners, to get a prediction more accurate and robust than any single model's.
Designing, developing, and deploying AI in ways that align with human values, fairness, transparency, and societal well-being.
AI programs that mimic human experts in a specific domain by applying if-then rules to a knowledge base of facts.
Methods that make an AI system's decisions and predictions understandable to humans instead of an opaque black box.
Training a model across many decentralized devices or servers that hold local data, without that data ever leaving its original location.
An approach where a model learns to recognize or perform a new task from only a small number of examples.
Taking a pre-trained model and training it further on task-specific or domain-specific data.
terms.note: The source page text was cut off for this entry, so the description is completed from its visible part and general meaning.

terms.description: Large models, often transformers, trained on vast and diverse data that can be adapted to many downstream tasks and applications.
A highly capable, general-purpose AI model at or near the leading edge of AI development.
AI systems that create new content such as text, images, music, code, or video; also called GenAI.
An architecture in which a generator and a discriminator network compete against each other to produce realistic synthetic data.
A family of large language models built on the transformer architecture that generate human-like text from input prompts.
A specialized chip, originally built to render graphics, that performs many mathematical calculations in parallel.
When an AI system produces information or responses that are incorrect, misleading, or entirely made up but presented as fact.
An approach to AI that puts human needs, values, and well-being first throughout development and deployment.
The way people operate and engage with computer systems.
AI systems that include human feedback or intervention as part of how they operate.
A parameter whose value is set before a machine learning model begins learning.
A large technology company that runs vast networks of data centers and can rapidly scale computing, storage, and cloud services on demand.
When a trained AI model makes predictions or decisions on new data it has not seen before.
How well humans can understand how an AI system reaches its decisions or predictions.
A simple, intuitive machine learning algorithm used for classification and regression.
A technique in which a smaller "student" model is trained to imitate the behavior and outputs of a larger, more complex "teacher" model.
terms.note: The source page text was cut off for this entry, so the description is completed from its visible part and general meaning.

terms.description: A structured database that represents information as a network of connected entities and the relationships between them.
An AI system trained on massive amounts of text to understand and generate human-like language.
A compressed, abstract mathematical space into which high-dimensional data such as images, text, or audio is encoded, capturing its essential features.
The practice of managing the full lifecycle of LLM-based applications in production.
A mathematical measure, also called a cost or objective function, of how far a model's predictions are from the correct values.
A branch of AI that lets computers learn patterns and make decisions from data without being explicitly programmed with rules.
A mathematical model of a sequence of events in which each next event's probability depends only on the current state, not on how it was reached.
Practices combining machine learning, software engineering, and DevOps to deploy, monitor, and maintain ML models reliably in production.
A simplified mathematical or computational representation of a real-world system, process, or relationship, used to make predictions or understand patterns.
A decline in a model's performance over time because real-world data has changed from the data it was trained on.
AI systems that can process, understand, and generate several kinds of data at once, such as text, images, audio, and video.
The branch of AI focused on enabling computers to understand, interpret, and generate human language meaningfully.
A computational model inspired by the human brain, made of interconnected layers of artificial neurons that process and pass on information.
A method that improves a machine learning model by adjusting its settings so it makes fewer mistakes.
When a model memorizes its training data too closely, including errors and random quirks, so it handles new data poorly.
An AI model whose weights, source code, training data (or a detailed auditable account of it), and development tools are available to download, run, inspect, reproduce, modify, and improve.
An AI model whose core components are publicly released so anyone can download it.
Software whose original design or blueprint is made freely available for anyone to see and use.
An internal variable of a machine learning model that is learned and adjusted during training.
Using data, statistical methods, and machine learning models to forecast future outcomes or trends.
The practice of carefully crafting instructions, or prompts, to guide language models toward the outputs you want.
A security attack that uses malicious input to trick a large language model into behaving in unintended ways.
A technique that improves language model outputs by letting the model look up external, up-to-date information before answering.
An AI system designed to solve complex problems by producing a logical, step-by-step chain of thought.
A type of machine learning where an agent improves through trial and error by taking actions in a specific environment.
The frameworks, principles, and practices that guide the ethical and safe development and deployment of AI.
The field combining engineering and computer science, now often with AI, to design and build machines that perform physical tasks.
The ability to understand and reason about the three-dimensional physical world, including how objects relate, move, and interact in space.
A training method where a model teaches itself by creating its own puzzles from raw data and then solving them.
Understanding the meaning of language by examining the relationships between words, phrases, and symbols.
Predictable mathematical relationships showing how AI performance improves as model size, training data, and computing power grow.
A machine learning approach where models are trained on labeled data, meaning inputs paired with correct outputs.
Artificially generated information created by algorithms or simulations rather than gathered from real-world events.
A container for numbers arranged in multiple dimensions, like a more advanced version of a spreadsheet.
Breaking text into smaller units called tokens, which can be words, word parts, or single characters, that language models can process.
Earlier approaches to AI that relied on explicitly programmed rules, logic, and human-defined knowledge instead of learning from data.
The collection of examples, such as text, images, or audio, used to teach a machine learning model how to do a task.
Reusing a model trained on one task as the starting point for a different but related task.
A neural network architecture that uses attention to understand relationships among all parts of the input at the same time instead of one step at a time.
A test proposed by Alan Turing in 1950 of whether a machine can show intelligent behavior indistinguishable from a human's.
A machine learning approach where models find patterns and structure in data that has no labels or predefined categories.
A specialized database built to store and efficiently search high-dimensional numerical vectors representing data such as text, images, or audio.
An adaptation of the transformer architecture, originally made for language, to process and analyze images.
The numerical parameters in a neural network that set the strength of connections between artificial neurons and shape how the model processes information.
A model's ability to handle tasks or categories it was never explicitly trained on, using its general knowledge.
